doc.title: Billy Bauer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

title: Davy Tough and Max Roach on keeping the groove
summary: Davy Tough and Max Roach each pushed the band to a place and stayed there, which Bauer says makes a good band.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: That’s right. And that’s what does it after a while. Well Davy was, he was like, it’s hard to say because he wasn’t a drummer that was a flashy drummer, you know or something. But he’d get into a certain place and he would just stay there, you couldn’t get him away from that, and the band would eventually get with him. With Max, I say that in the book too, like Max, when I played with him, I used to sit behind, down on 52nd Street, Charlie’s band was out there and then I was in the back with the other band that, we’d split it, so when I was in the back, all the kids when I was teaching in this conservatory, it’s called a conservatory, and they would say, “You’ve got to be cool, Daddy.” I says cool? Who’s cool? They says, “Yeah like Max Roach is cool.” I say, “Max Roach is cool?” I says I’m sitting behind him on the bandstand and boom a broken stick comes back.” I says, “He only feels like he’s cool, but he’s putting energy in there, you don’t just fall apart. It’s the feeling. So that’s what Max was doing. [scats] and he’d push it up, and when he’d get it right where he wanted it, then he’d stay there and he’d play. You know and he did that even when I was playing with groups like that All Star date, and then we did that big broadcast — well, a big broadcast — but it was one of them battle of the bands, you know. I didn’t think it was so good but evidently it’s still put out on the market. But Max was the same way there. He’d get it up to where he wanted it. Like in the beginning you think you can’t grab it, but then all of a sudden it levels off.
It felt like he was speeding up kind of, or just the intensity?

But I hate to say speeding up because he wasn’t speeding, it was just like a little anxiety you know, like it wasn’t where he wanted it. So and that’s what makes a good player or a good band. And the good player, when he’s in charge of us, if he’s got the right guys you know and they’re not mean or crazy or anything, but he just puts it in where he wants it to
be. That’s part of the make-up, no matter what he plays it’s in that groove. And that’s the hardest — well it isn’t the hard part, it’s easy, but if you’re looking for it you ain’t going to find it.
